description: Just a bunch of Student LARPers pretending to be software engineers. We're coming for the free food and Wi-Fi, and we held our NASA API calls together with duct tape and prayers.
summary:
SakaSAR is a browser-based agricultural climate-adaptation and flood-decision-support prototype built for the NASA Space Apps Challenge (Field Shift: Adapting Farms with NASA Data). It helps smallholder farmers, municipal agriculture officers, and disaster planners detect post-typhoon standing water and hidden root-zone drowning through heavy cloud cover that blinds optical satellites.

The platform combines Copernicus Sentinel-1 C-band radar backscatter with NASA NASADEM elevation, GPM IMERG rainfall, and SMAP soil moisture anomalies to compute an explainable 0–100 Field Drowning Risk index. It flags low, watch, and high alert parcels, translating them into plain-language 48-hour drainage actions and SMS alerts (≤160 characters).

For next-season planning, a PyTorch LSTM model trained on 25 years (2001–2026) of NASA POWER agro-climate records forecasts 1–7 day root-zone saturation and ranks three climate-resilient crop rotations (restorative legumes, deep-rooting cover crops, and short-cycle crops) matched to SoilGrids texture and farmer priorities. The 2D/3D MapLibre dashboard features Typhoon Kristine replay, downstream drainage tracing, and 100 m regional flood screening across all 114 Bicol municipalities at ₱0 data cost.
details:
THE PROBLEM

When a typhoon hits the Philippines, thick cloud stays over farmland for days. Optical satellites such as MODIS, VIIRS, Landsat and Sentinel-2 see nothing but white, just when farmers and local governments most need to know which fields are in trouble. The damage that follows is easy to misread. On day one after the storm the water drains off and the rice still looks green. Days later the leaf tips curl, a week on the field turns yellow, and then it dries out and browns. It looks like drought, but the field drowned. Roots sitting in waterlogged soil cannot get oxygen, stop taking up water, and the leaves wilt above wet ground. The damage starts on day one, long before anyone can see it. Published field trials put the average yield loss from waterlogging at about 23%, and much more at sensitive growth stages. Meanwhile, damage assessments in the Philippines still depend on manual field surveys that take weeks.

WHAT SakaSAR Does

SakaSAR is a free web dashboard (https://sakasar.earth) that answers four questions after a typhoon:

1. Where did floodwater stay, across a whole region?

2. Which individual fields are at risk of drowning, and what should the farmer do in the next 48 hours?

3. Which barangays and towns should agriculture and disaster teams visit first?

4. How long will roots stay waterlogged, and what should the farmer plant next season to adapt?

We built and tested it on a real event: Severe Tropical Storm Kristine (Trami), 21–26 October 2024. Our pilot is a strip of rice paddies in Barangays Taban, Bagongbong and Catanusan, Minalabac, Camarines Sur, in the Bicol River basin. We also ran the screening for all 114 municipalities of the Bicol Region.

HOW IT WORKS (STEP BY STEP)

Step 1 — See through the clouds with radar.

Sentinel-1 is a C-band synthetic aperture radar. It sends its own microwave signal, so it works at night and passes through cloud and rain. Calm open water reflects the signal away from the satellite and looks dark, while wetter soil changes how much signal comes back. We used Sentinel-1 RTC images (VV and VH) from Microsoft Planetary Computer. Each pixel's "normal" is the median of four calm passes (10 Aug, 22 Aug, 15 Sep and 27 Sep 2024), and the "after" image is 2 Nov 2024. We applied a Lee speckle filter, averaged to a shared 30 m grid, and computed the change in backscatter (ΔVV). A pixel counts as observed flood when it is darker than an Otsu-derived threshold (bounded to −20 to −12 dB), dropped at least 2 dB, sits on a slope under 5°, and is not permanent water in ESA WorldCover. As a quality check, the 9 October pass changed by only +0.31 dB from the baseline, so the 2 November signal is the storm, not seasonal noise. We rejected the storm-day pass (21 October) on purpose: typhoon winds roughened the water so much that permanent water brightened by a median of +5.3 dB and no longer looked like water.

Step 2 — Find where water collects, using NASA terrain.

From NASA's NASADEM elevation model we fill depressions (priority-flood), compute D8 flow directions and flow accumulation, and derive the Topographic Wetness Index (TWI). TWI shows where runoff gathers and where water has nowhere to go. We also trace the drainage corridor, so farmers can see where a ditch would help most.

Step 3 — Add the rain and the soil, using NASA data.

NASA GPM IMERG V07 gives 469 mm of rain in the event window plus 28 mm in the 7 days before; NASA POWER's 510 mm serves as an independent cross-check. NASA SMAP L4 root-zone soil moisture shows the soil was already +2.2 standard deviations wetter than its 30-day baseline, so the ground was primed to waterlog.

Step 4 — Score every field: the Field Drowning Risk.

Field Drowning Risk = 100 × (0.45 × radar wetness change + 0.35 × terrain wetness + 0.20 × rainfall), with each part scaled from 0 to 1. Scores of 70 and above are "high", 40–69 are "watch" and below 40 are "low". Built-up areas and permanent water are left unscored. In the pilot, 2 of 5 sample rice plots were rated high, 2 watch and 1 low, with 35.1 ha of flooded farmland observed by radar.

Step 5 — Check that it works, honestly.

Radar appears in both our score and the observed flood map, so checking the full score against that map would be circular. Instead we test the terrain + rain part of the model, which never sees the radar. In the pilot, it had already rated 31% of radar-flooded farmland high. Across all Bicol farmland at 100 m, it rated 92% of radar-flooded farmland high, against 50% of all farmland (1.85 times better than chance). A separate 200 m runoff and ponding score rated 95% of flooded farmland high, against 67% of all farmland. We report the honest number and say the circular one is only a consistency check.

Step 6 — Turn it into action.

- Farmer card: every plot gets its risk score, what drives it (radar, terrain, rain), a plain-language action such as digging a drainage trench, opening outlets or harvesting early, and an SMS alert of 160 characters or fewer that works on any basic phone.

- 4-stage advice timeline per plot: the next 48 hours, this week, before the next storm, and next season. Each stage names its data sources.

- LGU triage: barangays ranked by high-risk farm area (Taban → Bagongbong → Catanusan), all 114 Bicol towns ranked by flooded farmland (3,137 ha of 131,745 ha screened, with 100% radar coverage from two Sentinel-1 orbits), CSV export, and a printable one-page flood report per town.

Step 7 — Forecast how long roots stay waterlogged (our own AI model).

We trained a PyTorch LSTM neural network on 25 years (2001–2026) of NASA POWER daily weather (rain, temperature, humidity, sunlight) and soil wetness (GWETROOT, GWETTOP). It reads 30 days of history plus the coming week's rain and forecasts root-zone wetness for each of the next 7 days. The data was split by date: training 2001–2018, validation 2019–2021 and testing 2022–2026, so the model was tested on years it never saw. On the test years its error was 60% lower than "assume tomorrow equals today" and 25% lower than linear regression, rising to 77% lower in wet weeks, which are the ones that matter. For Kristine it forecast 7 of 7 waterlogged days, and the actual count was 7 of 7. Across all 31 NASA POWER cells in Bicol, its forecast issued on 3 November was right within one day in 28 of 31 cells. The model is small (about 19,600 parameters) and runs in under a millisecond, so it works on free hosting.

Step 8 — Adapt the farm for next season (the "Field Shift").

A rotation engine rates three strategies for each plot. It considers the plot's drowning risk, its SoilGrids 250 m soil texture and organic carbon, and the farmer's chosen priority (saving water, adding nitrogen, or earning cash):

- Restorative legume (mungbean/cowpea): fixes nitrogen and rebuilds organic matter.

- Deep-rooting bio-tillage cover crop (forage radish/sorghum-sudangrass): opens channels in the soil so water drains faster and ponding is reduced.

- Water-conserving short-cycle crop (pearl millet/sesame): uses less water and diversifies income.

Each option lists its benefits, its risks and what to check locally, such as seed supply, labour and buyer demand. When the priority changes, the ranking reorders. The farmer decides.

THE DASHBOARD

- Full-screen 3D map of Bicol (MapLibre GL JS) with our 30 m layers draped over terrain: risk score, risk class, TWI, ΔVV and slope.

- Day-by-day replay of Kristine: the NASA EONET storm track (closest pass about 259 km from Naga; Bicol flooded from the outer rain bands, not a direct hit), NASA POWER rain and soil-wetness heatmaps, and NASA GIBS imagery. The imagery shows that MODIS and VIIRS saw only cloud on 23 October, while the radar saw the flood.

- "This week" mode: current soil wetness across Bicol from the latest NASA POWER day, and how many days roots would stay waterlogged if a Kristine-sized storm hit now.

- "Check my field": a farmer or officer traces any parcel on the map and gets statistics from exactly the cells inside it.

- "Where does the water go?": traces the upstream catchment and downstream path from any point in Bicol.

- A rain what-if ("what if 150 mm fell?") on the runoff map.

- A 5-step Story mode for a guided demo, draggable windows, a full-screen workspace and a mobile layout.

- SakaSAR AI: an assistant that answers questions about the place and day on the map, grounded in SakaSAR's datasets (via the Groq API), with a rule-based fallback that works offline.

- An open FastAPI backend with documented endpoints (/docs) and downloadable CSV datasets.

BENEFITS AND IMPACT

- For farmers: warning within days that a field is drowning, before the leaves show it, while trenching, draining or early harvest can still save part of the crop, delivered in plain words and SMS-length text.

- For Municipal Agriculture Offices and MDRRMOs: a ranked list of where to go first, and a one-page flood report per town in hours instead of weeks of field surveys.

- For LGUs and the province: region-wide farmland screening (131,745 ha across 114 towns) in about 11 minutes, at ₱0 data cost, using only open NASA and Copernicus data.

- For long-term adaptation: one storm becomes a plan for next season. Rotations matched to soil and drowning risk help fields recover and cope better with the next typhoon, which is the heart of the Field Shift challenge.

- For other regions: the code is open source (MIT license), reproducible and runs offline from the included cache, so any typhoon-hit province can adapt it to its own area and storm.

TOOLS, CODING LANGUAGES, HARDWARE AND SOFTWARE

- Languages: Python, JavaScript, HTML, CSS

- Geospatial and science: NumPy, SciPy, rasterio/GDAL, shapely, pyproj; Lee speckle filter, Otsu thresholding, priority-flood depression filling, D8 flow routing, Topographic Wetness Index, bilinear interpolation

- Machine learning: PyTorch (LSTM soil-saturation forecast)

- Backend: FastAPI (REST API, OpenAPI docs)

- Frontend: MapLibre GL JS (3D terrain), Chart.js, Lucide icons

- AI assistant: Groq API, with an offline rule-based fallback

- Data access: Microsoft Planetary Computer STAC, Google Earth Engine (exports), NASA POWER API, NASA EONET API, NASA GIBS tiles

- Testing and deployment: pytest (31 automated tests), Playwright (browser checks and screenshots), Git/GitHub, Vercel (sakasar.earth)

- Hardware: ordinary student laptops. The LSTM trains in about 31 seconds on a CPU and the 30 m pilot rebuilds in about 1.5 seconds, with no paid compute or GPU needed.

- NASA data: NASADEM, GPM IMERG V07, SMAP L4, NASA POWER, NASA EONET, NASA GIBS (MODIS, VIIRS)

- Partner and other open data: Sentinel-1 RTC (ESA/Copernicus), ESA WorldCover 2021, ISRIC SoilGrids 250 m

HOW IT IS CREATIVE

- It reframes the problem: crop loss that looks like drought is often drowning that began on day one, and SakaSAR finds it while action still helps.

- It uses the right sensor at the right moment: radar during the storm when optical satellites are blind, then NASA terrain, rain, soil and a deep-learning forecast to read what the radar alone cannot.

- It fuses five kinds of data on one 30 m grid and ends with a text message a farmer can read, so the satellite science never stops at a map.

- It tests itself honestly: the headline accuracy comes from the part of the model that never saw the radar, and the dashboard openly states what it cannot do.

- It connects disaster response to adaptation: the same analysis that says "drain this field now" also says "here is what to plant next season, and why".

- It uses a past typhoon as proof, not as the limit: "This week" mode applies the same chain to today's soil conditions.

FACTORS OUR TEAM CONSIDERED

- Scientific honesty: C-band radar measures surface wetness, not root-zone moisture. Root-zone risk is inferred from radar, terrain and rain, and the dashboard says so. We do not claim L-band dielectric inversion, detection "7 days early" or specific water savings, because none of these was built or tested.

- Choosing a fair test site: our first pilot near Naga City sat on residential subdivisions, where radar cannot see water between buildings. A scan of the floodplain picked a strip with more than 60% cropland and less than 10% built-up land, and we placed the five sample plots evenly from west to east instead of choosing known flooded spots.

- Data quality: we rejected the storm-day radar pass after measuring that wind had hidden the water, and checked that pre-storm change was near zero.

- Resolution limits: NASA POWER cells are about 50 km across (regional soil, not a paddy sensor), and MODIS NDVI at 250 m is too coarse for small paddies. Plot outlines, households, crops and bare-field days are clearly labelled as sample values until LGU parcel and census data are available.

- Model limits: the risk weights are set by experts, not yet fitted to damage records, and the rotation rules are rules of thumb that every card asks the user to confirm with the Municipal Agriculture Office.

- Accessibility and low bandwidth: plain language, SMS-length alerts for basic phones, a mobile layout, fast loading from precomputed files, and free hosting.

- Cost and sustainability: ₱0 data licensing, open-source code, and fully offline reproducibility from cached data.

- Responsible AI: SakaSAR AI is grounded in our own datasets and falls back to rule-based answers. Our LSTM is our own model, trained on public NASA data and evaluated on held-out years.

- Future work, clearly separated from what is built: NISAR L-band radar for sensing through the crop canopy and deeper into the soil, 30 m Landsat/Sentinel-2 NDVI for crop calendars, ECOSTRESS heat-stress alerts, GRACE groundwater trends, calibrating weights against agriculture office damage reports, and real SMS delivery.
